pos: n. (the district of one of Solomon's twelve commissariat officers; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Arubboth, probably lattices or windows, from a root meaning to be latticed; named once in Scripture, at 1 Kings 4:10.
biblical_def: Aruboth is named once, as the district of the third of Solomon's twelve victualling officers: “The son of Hesed, in Aruboth; to him pertained Sochoh, and all the land of Hepher” (1 Kings 4:10). The name probably means lattices or windows. Like several officers in the register, the man is given only by his father's name, and his charge is described by the towns that went with it. The whole arrangement is set out at the head of the list: “And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision” (1 Kings 4:7). The districts were drawn by geography and not by tribe, which is itself a note worth taking: Solomon's administration cut across the old tribal lines, and the later division of the kingdom would show what that cost. One neighbouring charge gives the flavour of the whole: “Baana the son of Ahilud; to him pertained Taanach and Megiddo, and all Bethshean, which is by Zartanah beneath Jezreel, from Bethshean to Abelmeholah, even unto the place that is beyond Jokneam” (1 Kings 4:12). Aruboth with Sochoh and the land of Hepher was one slice of a kingdom at its height, fed by a schedule.

corruption_summary: The administrative structure of Solomon's kingdom is read as neutral efficiency, when the record itself shows districts cutting across the inheritance God had assigned by tribe.
corruption_paragraphs: Solomon's twelve districts do not follow the twelve tribes. They were drawn for supply, and the register in 1 Kings 4 shows it plainly. Efficient government is not a sin, but a kingdom that reorganises away from the inheritances God apportioned has loosened something, and the revolt under Rehoboam did not come out of nowhere. The Chronicler and the writer of Kings both leave the record where a reader can see it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's apportioning of an inheritance is not merely sentimental, and that administrative convenience is a poor reason to erase what He divided by lot.

pos: n. (a place to which the great valley of the Mount of Olives will reach in the day of the LORD; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Atsal, probably a side or a proximity, from a root meaning to be beside; named once in Scripture, at Zechariah 14:5.
biblical_def: Azal is named once, in one of the most arresting prophecies in the Old Testament: “And ye shall flee to the valley of the mountains; for the valley of the mountains shall reach unto Azal: yea, ye shall flee, like as ye fled from before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah: and the LORD my God shall come, and all the saints with thee” (Zechariah 14:5). The name probably means a side or a nearness, and the site is unidentified. What the verse describes is a geological rupture at the coming of the Lord: “And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east, and the mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst thereof toward the east and toward the west, and there shall be a very great valley” (Zechariah 14:4). The valley opened by that cleaving reaches to Azal, and the escaping remnant flees down it as men once fled an earthquake under Uzziah. The chapter's climax is the universal reign: “And the LORD shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD, and his name one” (Zechariah 14:9), and the nations that survive come up to worship: “every one that is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall even go up from year to year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts” (Zechariah 14:16).

corruption_summary: The bodily return of Christ is spiritualised into a figure, where Zechariah 14 puts His feet on a named hill and splits it.
corruption_paragraphs: “His feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives” is not the language of metaphor, and the valley that reaches to Azal is not an allegory of inward change. The dictionary holds the bodily second coming and the final judgment; it is open on the millennial question, which Reformed men have held in several ways, but it is not open on whether the Lord returns in a body to a place. He does, and a man who reads this chapter as a mood has read past the hill and the earthquake and the saints.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD shall be king over all the earth and His name one, and that the prophecy locates His coming at a hill a reader could walk up today.

pos: n. (a town in the district of Solomon's second commissariat officer; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elon Beth Chanan, the oak of the house of grace, compounding 'elon, an oak or terebinth, beth, a house, and chanan, grace or favour; named once in Scripture, at 1 Kings 4:9.
biblical_def: Elon-beth-hanan is named once, the last of four towns in one officer's charge: “The son of Dekar, in Makaz, and in Shaalbim, and Bethshemesh, and Elonbethhanan” (1 Kings 4:9). The name is a compound and a small sermon: the oak of the house of grace. Oaks and terebinths in Israel marked places of meeting, of burial, and sometimes of worship; a house of grace beside an oak is the kind of name a people give to ground where something was received rather than achieved. Nothing happened there that Scripture records. It appears in the supply register, under the son of Dekar, in the second of twelve districts set up so that “Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision” (1 Kings 4:7). The towns kept the king's table filled, and the system worked: “And those officers provided victual for king Solomon, and for all that came unto king Solomon's table, every man in his month: they lacked nothing” (1 Kings 4:27), down to the fodder: “Barley also and straw for the horses and dromedaries brought they unto the place where the officers were” (1 Kings 4:28).

corruption_summary: Place-names are read as decoration, when the names Israel gave her towns often confess what she believed about God.
corruption_paragraphs: A town called the oak of the house of grace is a confession fossilised in a map. Israel named her places for what God had done there — Bethel, Peniel, Jehovah-shammah, Ebenezer — and a people whose geography preaches has arranged its common life around its theology. The modern habit of naming developments for whatever sounds pleasant is not neutral; it simply confesses something else.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that grace is housed and not earned, and that a name recording it outlasted every other thing we know about the town.

pos: n. (the father of Eliezer the prophet, who rebuked Jehoshaphat for his alliance with Ahaziah)
etymology: Hebrew Dodavahu, beloved of the LORD, from dod, beloved or an uncle, with the divine name; named once in Scripture, at 2 Chronicles 20:37.
biblical_def: Dodavah is named once, as the father of a prophet: “Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the LORD hath broken thy works. And the ships were broken, that they were not able to go to Tarshish” (2 Chronicles 20:37). His name means beloved of the LORD. The occasion was the last recorded act of a good king's reign and a bad one: “And after this did Jehoshaphat king of Judah join himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly” (2 Chronicles 20:35). The venture was commercial: “And he joined himself with him to make ships to go to Tarshish: and they made the ships in Eziongeber” (2 Chronicles 20:36). God wrecked the fleet in the harbour. Jehoshaphat had already been rebuked once for marching with Ahab and had been told to his face that he loved them that hated the LORD; he did it again with Ahab's son, and the ships broke. The prophet's message is five words of doctrine — thou hast joined thyself, therefore the LORD hath broken — and it stands as the plainest statement in Chronicles of what an unequal alliance costs.

corruption_summary: Partnership with the ungodly is defended as pragmatism, where Chronicles reports that God broke the ships in the harbour.
corruption_paragraphs: Jehoshaphat was a genuinely reforming king who sent his princes out with the book of the law, and he twice yoked himself to the house of Ahab — once for war and once for trade. Both times a prophet was sent, and the second time the LORD simply destroyed the asset. The lesson is not that commerce is unclean but that a believer's partnerships are a matter of obedience, and that God may wreck a venture to break a friendship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD hath broken thy works is a sentence a true believer may hear, and that a man named beloved of the LORD fathered the prophet who had to say it.

pos: n. (a Netophathite whose sons came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ephay, probably birdlike or my bird, from 'oph, a bird or fowl; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 40:8.
biblical_def: Ephai is named once, as the father of men who came in to the governor Babylon had appointed over the ruins: “Then they came to Gedaliah to Mizpah, even Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, and the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah the son of a Maachathite, they and their men” (Jeremiah 40:8). His name probably derives from the word for a bird. The situation is the aftermath of the destruction of Jerusalem: “Now when all the captains of the forces which were in the fields, even they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land, and had committed unto him men, and women, and children, and of the poor of the land, of them that were not carried away captive to Babylon” (Jeremiah 40:7). What followed is one of the saddest sequences in the prophets. Gedaliah was warned: “Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not” (Jeremiah 40:14). He refused the warning and forbade the remedy: “Thou shalt not do this thing: for thou speakest falsely of Ishmael” (Jeremiah 40:16). Ishmael killed him.

corruption_summary: Charity is confused with credulity, where Gedaliah's refusal to believe a true warning cost him his life and scattered the remnant.
corruption_paragraphs: Gedaliah was a decent man and his generosity toward Ishmael was fatal. Scripture does not commend him for it; it records the warning, his refusal, and the murder. Charity that will not examine a credible report is not a virtue but a dereliction, and in a man holding office it endangers everyone under him. The remnant that had survived Babylon was scattered into Egypt because a governor would not believe what he was told.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a man in authority owes his people discernment as well as kindness, and that refusing to hear a true warning is itself a failure of love.

pos: n. (a head of a family of the Nethinim who returned from Babylon; spelled Hagaba at Nehemiah 7:48)
etymology: Hebrew Chagabah, a locust or grasshopper, from chagab; named at Ezra 2:45, and spelled Hagaba in the parallel list at Nehemiah 7:48.
biblical_def: Hagabah is the head of a family of the Nethinim, named in the register of those who came up out of Babylon: “The children of Lebanah, the children of Hagabah, the children of Akkub” (Ezra 2:45). The parallel roll in Nehemiah spells the same name Hagaba, and they are one family. The name means a locust or grasshopper. The Nethinim were the lowest order of temple servants, given to the Levites for the menial work of the house: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Ezra 2:43) begins their list, and it runs for a dozen verses of names nobody has ever preached on. That God kept these households by name through seventy years of captivity, and brought them back to the same service, is the quiet argument of the chapter. The settlement at the end puts every order in its place: “So the priests, and the Levites, and some of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities” (Ezra 2:70). A family called Grasshopper went home to carry wood and water for the house of God.

corruption_summary: Menial service in the house of God is counted negligible, where Ezra keeps the household names of the lowest order of temple servants through a seventy-year captivity.
corruption_paragraphs: The Nethinim did the heavy work. They are listed by family, by name, and in order, and their names survived Babylon. A church that ranks its members by visibility has a different accounting from the one in Ezra 2, where the men who carried the wood are entered in the same register as the priests and brought home to the same city.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God preserved the households of His lowest servants by name, and that the order which put every family in its own city was His order and not an accident of resettlement.

pos: n. (a storehouse or gathering-place at the south of the temple, assigned to the porters)
etymology: Hebrew 'asuppim, gatherings or collections, from 'asaph, to gather; the Authorized Version margin at 1 Chronicles 26:15 gives “Heb. gatherings.”
biblical_def: Asuppim occurs twice, both times in the assignment of the temple gates to the porters. First: “To Obededom southward; and to his sons the house of Asuppim” (1 Chronicles 26:15). Then in the detail of the watch: “Eastward were six Levites, northward four a day, southward four a day, and toward Asuppim two and two” (1 Chronicles 26:17). The Hebrew means gatherings — the Authorized Version says so in its own margin — and the house of Asuppim was evidently a storehouse where the collections brought to the temple were kept. It had its own guard, two by two. The chapter is a staffing plan for the house of God, and it says what the plan was for: “Among these were the divisions of the porters, even among the chief men, having wards one against another, to minister in the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 26:12). Even the lots are recorded: “To Shuppim and Hosah the lot came forth westward, with the gate Shallecheth, by the causeway of the going up, ward against ward” (1 Chronicles 26:16). Doorkeeping is called ministering in the house of the LORD, and guarding the money is part of it.

corruption_summary: Guarding the church's money is treated as administration rather than ministry, where Chronicles calls the porters' work ministering in the house of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: David set a watch of two and two toward the storehouse, and the chapter calls the whole arrangement ministering in the house of the LORD. Scripture takes the custody of what God's people give with complete seriousness — Paul would later travel with appointed men so that no man should blame him in the matter of the collection. A church that handles money without guards and without accounting has not become more spiritual; it has abandoned a duty Chronicles treats as worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that doorkeeping and storekeeping in God's house are named as ministry, and that the men who did it were assigned by lot and set in order ward against ward.

pos: n. (a name in the Song of Solomon, whose chariots the bride names; occurs once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Amminadib, my people is willing, or my willing people, compounding 'am, a people, with nadib, willing or noble; named once in Scripture, at Song of Solomon 6:12.
biblical_def: Amminadib occurs once, in a verse that has puzzled every translator who has handled it: “Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib” (Song of Solomon 6:12). The Hebrew compounds the word for a people with the word for willing or noble, so that the name reads my people is willing — the same root that gives Israel the freewill offering. Whether it is a proper name or a phrase to be translated has been argued for centuries, and the Authorized Version keeps it as a name. The force of the line is unmistakable even where its grammar is hard: the bride is caught up suddenly, before she is aware, and carried as by a chariot. The verse before sets the scene in a garden: “I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded” (Song of Solomon 6:11), and the verse after is a calling back: “Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies” (Song of Solomon 6:13). A willing people, a sudden carrying away, and a bride who looks like two armies.

corruption_summary: A hard verse is either smoothed away or made to carry a certainty it cannot bear; honest exposition says what is clear and marks what is not.
corruption_paragraphs: Song of Solomon 6:12 is genuinely difficult, and the dictionary says so. That is not the same as the soft-pedalling this work rejects elsewhere: Scripture is perspicuous in all that is necessary for salvation, and that doctrine was never a claim that every clause is equally plain. The honest course is to state what the verse plainly conveys — a sudden, unlooked-for carrying away of the soul — and to mark the grammar as disputed rather than manufacture a confident paraphrase.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the willingness of God's people is itself His gift, and that the soul is often carried further than it knew it had consented to go.

pos: n. (a Syrian woman; used once, of the concubine of Manasseh who bore Machir)
etymology: English feminine formed on Aramite, a Syrian, from Hebrew 'Aram, Syria; used once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 7:14.
biblical_def: Aramitess means a Syrian woman, and the word is used once: “The sons of Manasseh; Ashriel, whom she bare: ( but his concubine the Aramitess bare Machir the father of Gilead” (1 Chronicles 7:14). The verse is awkward in the English because the Chronicler is compressing two households into one parenthesis, and it continues: “And Machir took to wife the sister of Huppim and Shuppim, whose sister's name was Maachah;) and the name of the second was Zelophehad: and Zelophehad had daughters” (1 Chronicles 7:15). What the verse quietly records is that Machir, from whom the whole half-tribe of Manasseh east of Jordan descended, was the son of a Syrian concubine. The line is traced forward without apology: “And the sons of Ulam; Bedan. These were the sons of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 7:17). Scripture repeatedly records foreign women in Israel's lines — Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, this Syrian — and does not treat their presence as a blemish to be managed. It does not commend concubinage; it reports it, as it reports Jacob's and David's, and it leaves the practice condemned by the creation ordinance it everywhere assumes.

corruption_summary: Concubinage in the patriarchal narratives is read as divine approval, where Scripture reports the practice and condemns it by the creation ordinance it never revokes.
corruption_paragraphs: Manasseh had a concubine, as Abraham and Jacob and David did, and Scripture records the children. Reporting is not commendation. Marriage is one man and one woman from Genesis 2 forward, and the Lord grounds His own teaching on divorce in that original ordinance rather than in the patriarchs' practice. Every polygamous household in Scripture is also a household in visible trouble, which is the narrative's own commentary.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God brought a half-tribe of Israel out of a Syrian woman's son and wrote it down plainly, and that He is not ashamed of the foreigners in His people's lines.

pos: n. (a king of the Ammonites who sent Ishmael to assassinate Gedaliah; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Ba'alis, probably containing ba'al, lord or master; named once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 40:14.
biblical_def: Baalis is named once, as the foreign king behind the murder that finished off the remnant left in Judah: “And said unto him, Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not” (Jeremiah 40:14). His name probably carries the element ba'al, lord. The warning came from Johanan and the captains who had gathered to Gedaliah at Mizpah after Babylon appointed him governor over “men, and women, and children, and of the poor of the land, of them that were not carried away captive to Babylon” (Jeremiah 40:7). Johanan offered to deal with Ishmael quietly, and Gedaliah forbade him: “Thou shalt not do this thing: for thou speakest falsely of Ishmael” (Jeremiah 40:16). The warning was true. Ishmael killed Gedaliah at a meal, and the survivors fled into Egypt against Jeremiah's express word, which is where the book of Jeremiah leaves them. Ammon had been Israel's enemy since the judges, and the last blow Ammon struck was through a Jewish assassin, against the one arrangement that might have kept a remnant in the land.

corruption_summary: Political violence is read as the working out of competing interests only, when Jeremiah names the foreign king who paid for it and the man who ignored the warning.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is specific about conspiracies. It names Baalis, it names his agent, it names the men who brought the warning, and it records the governor's refusal. The result was that the remnant went down into Egypt in direct defiance of the prophet, and the last chapters of Jeremiah are the record of it. God's providence governed the whole, and every man in it acted freely and answered for what he did.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's sovereign ordering of a nation's end leaves every conspirator and every negligent officer fully accountable for his own part.
